analysis.one_liner: Makes it much harder for large banks to win government approval for mergers.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with zero cosponsors, never received a committee hearing or floor vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the rules for approving bank mergers. Regulators would have to find that a merger's benefits to the public outweigh its costs, weighing branch closures, job losses, and effects on local economies. Banks with poor community-lending records could be denied, big mergers would face stress tests and tougher competition review, banks would have to disclose their private dealings with regulators, and ordinary citizens would gain the right to sue to block an approved merger.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary banking customers, especially in communities hit by branch closures; small businesses and homebuyers who depend on local lending competition; bank employees whose jobs are lost in mergers; and taxpayers, who currently absorb the risk when banks grow so large that failure would threaten the financial system.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Bank customers, small borrowers, and bank employees

how_it_helps.text: Regulators could not approve a merger unless the public benefits outweigh the expected costs, and they would have to weigh branch closures, employment losses, and effects on the cost and availability of financial services [S3].

A merger could be denied if the largest bank involved had anything less than an 'outstanding' Community Reinvestment Act rating, and large banks would have to file community benefits plans with measurable lending goals for low- and moderate-income communities [S3].

Companies over $100 billion would face stress tests to prove they could survive a severe downturn, and regulators would apply heightened scrutiny in any local market where the merger substantially increases banking concentration [S3].

Banks would have to disclose all their communications with regulators about a merger, and their CEOs would have to certify under penalty that no one sought or received backdoor assurances of approval [S3].

Any individual could sue in federal court to challenge a merger approval on an expedited basis, without having to pay the agencies' or banks' legal costs, and the merger could not close until the court ruled [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large banks and bank holding companies — particularly those over $10 billion or $100 billion in assets — which would face tougher approval standards, higher capital requirements, slower and more public merger reviews, and a new litigation risk. Big-bank shareholders bear the cost in deal-making freedom and executive accountability.

drawbacks.text: The bill applies its cost-benefit test to mergers of all sizes, which could slow down combinations of small or troubled banks that regulators currently wave through quickly, potentially complicating resolutions of failing banks [S3].

Giving any individual standing to sue, with the merger frozen until the court rules within 30 days on a fresh ('de novo') review, could delay even well-founded mergers and invite repeat litigation [S3].
The bill contains an escape hatch: the Financial Stability Oversight Council could approve otherwise barred mergers on a two-thirds vote if it deems them necessary for financial stability [S3].
Banks would bear new compliance costs — certified disclosures, community benefits plans, updated public filings within two business days of any regulator contact [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefits are real but indirect: fewer bank consolidations mean more local branches, more small-business and mortgage lending competition, and less 'too big to fail' risk. The costs fall on the regulated industry in compliance and deal friction, plus some risk that honest small-bank mergers get tangled in process. The citizen-suit provision and de novo review are broad enough that courts could see heavy use, which is the strongest good-faith objection. On balance the bill aimed at a genuine problem — bank regulators approving nearly all mergers with minimal scrutiny — and its design, while aggressive, matched that problem.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Financial Services Committee in September 2021, but the committee never took it up and it died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023 [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Representative Chuy Garcia introduced the Bank Merger Review Modernization Act of 2021 on September 29, 2021, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day [S1][S5].
No member signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
The bill received no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large banks and their shareholders: by dying without a hearing, the bill left the existing merger-approval regime — where regulators historically approve the overwhelming majority of bank deals — untouched, so bank consolidation and the deal-making freedom of large banks continued unchanged.

for.name: Rep. Jesus G. 'Chuy' Garcia
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Financial Services Committee.

against.name: Rep. Maxine Waters
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee hearing or markup during the 117th Congress.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; it received no hearing or vote.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill drew zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan pattern can be read from the record [S4].

industries.industry: Large banks and bank holding companies
industries.note: The bill would have made merger approval far harder for banks over $10 billion and $100 billion, adding cost-benefit tests, stress tests, 'outstanding' community-lending requirements, disclosure of regulator contacts, and citizen lawsuits. Because these banks profit from consolidation — closing branches, cutting staff, and gaining market power over borrowers — their interest ran against the bill's beneficiaries. The bill died, so nothing changed for them.

Community banks under $10 billion were largely exempt from the new capital and stress-test requirements, and stricter review of big-bank mergers could preserve local competition they rely on. But the cost-benefit and competition tests applied to all mergers, including acquisitions of small banks, adding friction for sellers.
